identification.summary: Coral Sleet (formerly Storm-1877) is Microsoft's name for a North Korean state actor. Microsoft groups it with Sapphire Sleet and Jasper Sleet as actors that often use financial-opportunity or job-interview lures to get initial access [S1]. Microsoft first described Storm-1877 in May 2024. It said the actor had used malicious npm packages since late 2023 to deliver JavaScript-based malware to software developers, and that Palo Alto Networks publicly reported this campaign as 'Contagious Interview' [S2]. Unit 42 first reported Contagious Interview in November 2023: fake employers persuade job seekers to install malware during online interviews, using the BeaverTail stealer/loader and the InvisibleFerret Python backdoor [S5]. In March 2026 Microsoft reported that Coral Sleet used AI coding tools to build and iterate malware components, including the OtterCookie malware, and used agentic AI for end-to-end lure development and infrastructure provisioning [S1]. In September 2026 Japanese, US, Australian and German agencies published a joint advisory on the same activity cluster (as 'WaterPlum' / Contagious Interview). The advisory, as reported, said the actors infected at least 30,000 devices in more than 100 countries and took funds or credentials from more than 7,000 cryptocurrency wallets [S11].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft says the Contagious Interview campaign has been active since at least December 2022 [S4]. Microsoft says Storm-1877 used malicious npm packages since late 2023 [S2]. Unit 42's first public report was November 2023 [S5], and ESET says the overlapping DeceptiveDevelopment cluster has been active since at least November 2023 [S7].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Coral Sleet. Microsoft explicitly gives 'Coral Sleet (formerly Storm-1877)' [S1]. Microsoft maps Storm-1877 to the npm campaign Palo Alto calls Contagious Interview [S2]. Unit 42 tracks Contagious Interview as CL-STA-0240 [S5][S6]. NTT Security tracks the cluster as WaterPlum and equates it with CL-STA-0240, DeceptiveDevelopment, DEV#POPPER, Famous Chollima, PurpleBravo and Tenacious Pungsan, as reported [S8]. ESET's DeceptiveDevelopment overlaps with Contagious Interview, DEV#POPPER, Famous Chollima, PurpleBravo and Tenacious Pungsan, as reported [S7][S13]. Trend Micro associates its Void Dokkaebi intrusion set, also known as Famous Chollima, with this campaign cluster [S10]. CLUSTER BOUNDARY: Microsoft tracks North Korean remote IT workers separately as Jasper Sleet (formerly Storm-0287). It says Storm-1877 is one of several other DPRK clusters that also pursue fraudulent employment [S3]. Unit 42 likewise separates the job-seeker IT-worker campaign Wagemole (CL-STA-0241) from Contagious Interview [S5]. CrowdStrike's Famous Chollima covers both the recruiter and IT-worker activity, so it is broader than Coral Sleet. The imported summary on this record describes WageMole (IT-worker fraud), which better matches Jasper Sleet than Coral Sleet. Microsoft's March 2026 Contagious Interview post describes the campaign but does not name Coral Sleet [S4].

attribution.sponsor: Democratic People's Republic of Korea. Microsoft describes Coral Sleet as a North Korean threat actor [S1]. The September 2026 multinational advisory, as reported, assesses (per Japan's National Police Agency and the FBI) that WaterPlum operators and some North Korean IT workers fall under the 313 General Bureau of the Munitions Industry Department of the Workers' Party of Korea Central Committee [S11][S12].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft names Coral Sleet as North Korean but gives no confidence level in the cited post [S1]. SentinelLABS attributes the CTI-platform activity it observed to North Korean Contagious Interview actors with high confidence [S9]. The 313 General Bureau assessment is from the NPA and FBI (government), as reported in press coverage. It was made against the WaterPlum / Contagious Interview cluster, not against Microsoft's Coral Sleet designation by name [S11][S12].
attribution.basis: Microsoft Threat Intelligence telemetry and reporting [S1][S2][S3]; Unit 42 telemetry and malware analysis [S5][S6]; ESET, NTT, SentinelLABS/Validin and Trend Micro vendor research [S7][S8][S9][S10]; joint government advisory from Japan, the US, Australia and Germany (reported via press) [S11][S12].

objectives: Revenue generation for the DPRK through cryptocurrency theft. The 2026 joint advisory, as reported, says the actors took funds or credentials from more than 7,000 crypto wallets and moved about $10.7 million (about 1.7 billion yen) to North Korea [S11][S12]. Unit 42 assessed the goals as stealing cryptocurrency and using compromised targets as staging environments for future attacks [S5]. Microsoft notes the actors harvest API tokens, cloud credentials, signing keys, crypto wallets and password-manager artifacts. A compromised developer could therefore become a route into the employer's environment or software supply chain [S4][S11].

sectors: Software developers and job seekers in the technology sector [S2][S5]
Developers at enterprise solution providers and media and communications firms [S4]
regions: Global: at least 30,000 devices in more than 100 countries (December 2025 to July 2026, per the joint advisory as reported) [S11]
Japan, United States, Australia and Germany were the co-authoring governments [S11][S12]
targeting.notes: Targeting is individual-centric. The actors approach developers through fake recruiter personas, job postings on platforms such as LinkedIn and Upwork, and fake coding tests. Victim organizations are then exposed through the individual's device [S4][S7][S11]. SentinelLABS counted over 230 victims between January and March 2025 and said the true figure is likely higher [S9]. Recruiter lures have posed as cryptocurrency trading firms and AI solution providers [S4].

capabilities.summary: Social engineering through fake recruiters and technical interviews. Victims are asked to clone and run booby-trapped repositories (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket), install malicious npm packages, or follow 'quick fix' steps for supposed video-conferencing errors [S2][S4][S11]. Malware: the BeaverTail JavaScript stealer and loader, and the InvisibleFerret Python backdoor, which supports keylogging, file exfiltration and remote access via AnyDesk [S5][S6][S7]. Unit 42 reported Qt-compiled BeaverTail builds for Windows and macOS from July 2024 [S6]. Later families: the OtterCookie JavaScript backdoor (v3 and v4 in February and April 2025; v4 added VM detection and Chrome/MetaMask credential theft), a JavaScript beaconing agent, FlexibleFerret, and VS Code task-file abuse that runs code when a project is trusted [S4][S8]. The joint advisory coverage also lists OtterCandy and StoatWaffle [S11]. Microsoft says Coral Sleet uses AI coding tools to generate and revise malware, including OtterCookie, and uses agentic AI for lure websites and remote infrastructure provisioning [S1]. The operators watch threat intelligence platforms (Validin, VirusTotal) to spot their own exposed infrastructure and stand up replacements quickly [S9].

campaigns.name: Contagious Interview campaign begins
campaigns.summary: Microsoft says the fake developer-interview campaign has been active since at least December 2022.

campaigns.name: Contagious Interview and Wagemole disclosed (Unit 42)
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 reports Contagious Interview (CL-STA-0240), which uses fake employers to deliver BeaverTail and InvisibleFerret to job seekers. It reports the separate IT-worker campaign Wagemole (CL-STA-0241) alongside it.

campaigns.name: Microsoft names Storm-1877
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reports that Storm-1877 has used malicious npm packages against software developers since late 2023, and maps it to Palo Alto's Contagious Interview.

campaigns.name: Cross-platform BeaverTail update
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 reports continued fake-recruiter activity with updated BeaverTail (Qt builds for Windows and macOS) and InvisibleFerret.

campaigns.name: DeceptiveDevelopment targets freelance developers (ESET)
campaigns.summary: ESET reports fake job postings and trojanized coding projects delivering BeaverTail and InvisibleFerret to freelance developers.

campaigns.name: OtterCookie v4 and Russian infrastructure
campaigns.summary: NTT reports OtterCookie v3 and v4 with added credential theft and VM detection. Trend Micro reports Void Dokkaebi using Russian IP ranges in Khasan and Khabarovsk behind VPN, proxy and RDP layers.

campaigns.name: Operators caught monitoring CTI platforms
campaigns.summary: SentinelLABS and Validin report that Contagious Interview operators registered Validin accounts and used VirusTotal from March to June 2025 to track exposure of their infrastructure. More than 230 victims were counted for January to March 2025.

campaigns.name: AI-enabled tradecraft and Microsoft Contagious Interview report
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reports Coral Sleet's AI-assisted malware development (OtterCookie) and agentic lure and infrastructure workflows. A separate Microsoft post details OtterCookie, the beaconing agent and VS Code task abuse.

campaigns.name: Multinational WaterPlum advisory
campaigns.summary: Japan, the US, Australia and Germany report at least 30,000 infected devices in over 100 countries (December 2025 to July 2026), more than 7,000 affected crypto wallets and about $10.7M moved to the DPRK. They attribute the activity to the 313 General Bureau (reported via press).

diamond.adversary: North Korean state actor (Microsoft: Coral Sleet, formerly Storm-1877) [S1]. NPA and FBI assess the WaterPlum operators fall under the 313 General Bureau of the Munitions Industry Department, as reported [S12]. Operators work in coordinated teams [S9].
diamond.capability: Fake-recruiter social engineering. Malware includes BeaverTail, InvisibleFerret, OtterCookie, OtterCandy, StoatWaffle and FlexibleFerret, delivered through npm packages, trojanized repositories and VS Code tasks. Malware is developed with AI assistance [S1][S4][S5][S8][S11].
diamond.infrastructure: Public code hosting (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket) and the npm registry; fake interview and company websites built on development platforms; URL shorteners redirecting to vercel.app [S1][S4]. Russian IP ranges behind VPN, proxy and RDP layers [S10]. Infrastructure is replaced quickly after exposure [S9].
diamond.victim: Software developers, freelancers, and Web3/crypto professionals, and their employers [S4][S7][S9][S11]. At least 30,000 devices in more than 100 countries [S11].
diamond.socioPolitical: Sanctions-evasion revenue for the DPRK through crypto theft. The advisory links the activity to the same bureau as DPRK IT workers [S11][S12].
diamond.technology: Developer workstations holding credentials, signing keys, cloud tokens and wallets. Trust in code repositories, package managers, IDE automation (VS Code tasks) and remote hiring workflows [S4][S11].

gaps: Microsoft has not published a dedicated Coral Sleet profile in the sources gathered. The Coral Sleet = Storm-1877 equivalence rests on one sentence in the March 2026 AI-tradecraft post [S1]. Microsoft's March 2026 Contagious Interview post does not name the actor [S4].

Cluster boundaries: Microsoft says Storm-1877 also pursues fraudulent employment [S3], and its March 2026 post groups Coral Sleet with Jasper Sleet [S1]. It is unclear how much IT-worker (WageMole) activity Microsoft folds into Coral Sleet versus Jasper Sleet. The imported record summary (WageMole) may belong to Jasper Sleet.

The September 2026 joint advisory primary text (FBI IC3 / NPA) could not be opened. Figures and the 313 General Bureau attribution come from press coverage [S11][S12]. The advisory names the cluster WaterPlum, not Coral Sleet.
Unit 42, SentinelLABS, Trend Micro, ESET and NTT primary reports could not be fetched (host blocked). Their content is taken from search-result summaries and press coverage.
MITRE ATT&CK G1052 page could not be fetched to confirm its group name and associated-group list.
No Microsoft confidence level for the Coral Sleet North Korea attribution was found.

Aliases Gwisin Gang, Nickel Tapestry, TAG-121 and UNC5267 in the imported record were not confirmed against cited sources for this cluster. Some (for example UNC5267) are commonly used for IT-worker activity.
ContagiousDrop tooling and the face-swap/deepfake claims in some advisory coverage were not verified against primary sources.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is people, not networks. Individual developers and Web3 personnel on LinkedIn and Upwork, their personal and work devices, and the code repositories, npm registry and IDE automation they trust [S4][S7][S11]. DoD-adjacent software contractors and personnel using personal devices for job searches fall in scope. STEP 2 (effects): A single compromised developer exposes cloud tokens, signing keys and credentials that can be pivoted into the employer and its software supply chain [S4][S11]. AI-assisted development shortens the actor's retooling cycle [S1]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Recruiter persona approach, then a fake coding test or 'fix your camera' instruction, then a malicious repo, npm package or VS Code task, then BeaverTail or OtterCookie, then InvisibleFerret or a beaconing agent, then credential and wallet theft [S4][S5][S6][S8]. Infrastructure is replaced when CTI platforms expose it [S9]. STEP 4: MLCOA is high-volume, opportunistic theft of cryptocurrency and credentials from developers worldwide [S11]. MDCOA is pivoting from a compromised contractor developer into a defense software supply chain via stolen signing keys or cloud credentials, or handing access to other DPRK units [S4][S5]. Candidate indicators: unsolicited recruiter contact leading to repo clone or npm install on a work device; node or python child processes spawned from VS Code tasks.json; outbound connections to vercel.app or short-link redirects from developer hosts; AnyDesk installed unexpectedly; bulk reads of browser credential and wallet extension stores [S4][S5][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Fuse identity, endpoint and developer-tooling telemetry (IDE task execution, package installs) into the common operational picture. Network-centric sensors alone will miss an intrusion that starts on a personal or contractor device [S4]. (2) Authorities: The initial compromise usually occurs off the DODIN, on personal or contractor endpoints. Response depends on coordination with FBI, DC3 (a co-sealer of the 2026 advisory) and DIB CS partners rather than DoD-internal authorities alone [S11][S12]. (3) Mission assurance: Treat code-signing keys, CI/CD secrets and cloud tokens on developer workstations as mission-critical assets. Rotate them after any suspected Contagious Interview exposure [S4]. (4) Coordination: The cluster has many vendor names (Coral Sleet, Contagious Interview, WaterPlum, DeceptiveDevelopment, Famous Chollima), and some of these names also cover IT-worker activity. Normalize names on the Microsoft designation in reporting, and coordinate with allied partners (Japan, Australia, Germany) who co-authored the advisory [S1][S8][S11].

provenance.importedSummary: WageMole is a North Korean state-sponsored APT that employs social engineering and technology to secure remote job opportunities in Western countries, leveraging stolen personal data from the Contagious Interview campaign. Threat actors create fake identities, including passports and driver's licenses, and prepare study guides for interviews, often utilizing generative AI for well-structured responses. They target small to mid-sized businesses and utilize job platforms like Upwork and Indeed, while employing automation scripts for account creation. WageMole's activities include sharing code within their group and requesting payments through platforms like PayPal to conceal their identity.
